 Cop31 Cop31 as it happened: Fossil fuels dumped from latest draft deal at climate summit
 New draft decision omits cause of climate crisis in blow to vulnerable countries on penultimate day of UN climate talks
  Updated  22h ago Ajit Niranjan (now) and Matthew Pearce (earlier) Thu 19 Nov 2026 11.09 EST First published on Thu 19 Nov 2026 02.07 EST Share Key events 22h ago Day 11 of Cop31 – recapped 
 23h ago US, China and Russia agree to pump more oil 
 24h ago Panama to block any outcome without a cap on oil production 
 1d ago Fossil fuels dumped from latest draft deal 
 1d ago IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, top researcher says 
 1d ago Deep divisions persist as climate talks begin penultimate day 
 The Cop presidents Chris Bowen and Murat Kurum leave a press conference about the most recent draft of the cover text, which omitted any mention of fossil fuels. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Cop presidents Chris Bowen and Murat Kurum leave a press conference about the most recent draft of the cover text, which omitted any mention of fossil fuels. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images Ajit Niranjan (now) and Matthew Pearce (earlier) Thu 19 Nov 2026 11.09 EST First published on Thu 19 Nov 2026 02.07 EST Share From 22h ago 11.09 EST Day 11 of Cop31 – recapped
 That’s all for today. Here are the highlights from the 11th day of the 31st UN climate summit:
 Delaying the IPCC report will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, a top researcher said
 “Climate action and development and progress are not mutually exclusive,” the president-designate of next year’s Cop told the Guardian
 Fossil fuels were dropped from the latest draft deal, prompting outrage from campaigners
 Panama told the Presidency it would block any outcome that does not meet demands including a cap on oil production
 At a separate meeting in Shenzhen, the US, China and Russia agree to pump more oil 
 Thanks for following – we’ll be back tomorrow for the final scheduled day of the summit.

 23h ago US, China and Russia agree to pump more oil 
 24h ago Panama to block any outcome without a cap on oil production 
 1d ago Fossil fuels dumped from latest draft deal 
 1d ago IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, top researcher says 
 1d ago Deep divisions persist as climate talks begin penultimate day 
 22h ago 10.56 EST Asked about today’s commitment by the US, China and Russia to boost oil production – and the lack of engagement in the Cop process from the two biggest polluters, the US and China – Chris Bowen said China was engaging constructively at Cop31 . The president of the Cop31 negotiations, speaking at a press conference earlier today, said: “China is raising – as they should – their issues and concerns. But they’re coming at this conversation in a spirit of helping us make it work, and a spirit of positive engagement.”
 Share 22h ago 10.47 EST Graham Readfearn Collecting pictures of royalty is not usually a hobby of mine, but now I have two from these talks in Antalya.
 View image in fullscreen The queen of Malaysia, Raja Zarith Sofiah, will officially close her country’s pavilion today. Photograph: Graham Readfearn, the Guardian On my way to the Australia pavilion this morning, the UN police officers blocked a path for the queen of Malaysia, Raja Zarith Sofiah, who has been here for a couple of days and will officially close her country’s pavilion today.
 Last week, I watched Queen Mary of Denmark (who is actually from Tasmania in Australia) give a speech about the importance of electrification at the opening of the Denmark pavilion.
 View image in fullscreen Queen Mary of Denmark gave a speech about the importance of electrification at the opening of the Denmark pavilion. Photograph: Graham Readfearn, the Guardian If there are other royals who have been here but I have missed, may I offer your country my humblest apologies.
 [Bows and leaves the blog]
 Share 22h ago 10.37 EST Fiona Harvey Ireland holds the revolving presidency of the EU, and so as well as leading on negotiations at Cop31 is in charge of its press conferences, public events and the hosting of meetings. As a result, the EU’s main suite of meeting rooms at this year’s Cop are named after Irish writers.
 The choice of writers is telling. Cops might make some think of lines from poet WB Yeats – “All changed, changed utterly:/A terrible beauty is born” – or his fellow Nobel laureate, the artist of futility, Samuel Beckett – “Let’s go.” “We can’t.” “Why not?” “We’re waiting for Godot.”
 Instead, Ireland has gone with two women and two men. Eavan Boland, who died in 2020, was a poet who foregrounded women’s experiences, in contrast to the male-dominated literature of the era. In her room, negotiators might recall the former Irish president Mary Robinson’s contention that the climate crisis is “caused by men, but falls most heavily on women”.
 In the Maeve Binchy room, guests might be expected to entertain fond romantic hopes of a harmonious and happy ending to Cop.
 Jonathan Swift, one of the two chosen male writers, is most famous for the satire Gulliver’s Travels, but also wrote scathingly on the desperate plight of the poor and the indifference of the rich to their suffering, which might resonate with developing countries here.
 But when the draft text undergoes its final iterations, in a thicket of square brackets, contested commas, impenetrable jargon and convoluted coinages, surely the teams will repair to the James Joyce room. The author of Ulysses and Finnegans Wake might feel strangely at home at a Cop.
 View image in fullscreen Cop31 climate summit continues in Turkey’s Antalya. Photograph: Mehmet Emin Menguarslan/Anadolu/Getty Images Share 23h ago 10.14 EST Gabrielle Canon Nature-focused advocates were largely optimistic even after the dismally received second draft.
 “It took almost 30 years to secure explicit reference to fossil fuels in the finalised Cop text – now Cop31 risks eliminating that progress overnight,” said John Verdieck, the Director of International Climate Policy at The Nature Conservancy.
 “However, while fossil fuels tend to overhang everything at climate COPs – with good reason – what happens between these meetings and on the ground also matters,” he said, pointing to potential for progress, particularly on Brazil’s deforestation roadmap and The Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), a conservation finance initiative that provides incentives for countries to keep tropical forests healthy. Those aspects “give cause for hope at an otherwise underwhelming Cop31,” he added.
 View image in fullscreen An illegal mining camp in a deforested area of Roraima State, Brazil, in 2023. Photograph: Alan Chaves/AFP/Getty Images Chris Dragisic, the National Audubon Society’s Managing Director for Global Policy, agreed, highlighting the enormous amount of work and diplomacy happening away from the negotiating table.
 “We want to see things be as strong as possible in the Covered Decision text, but when things aren’t recognised here, it doesn’t mean that there’s no real world action possible,” she said, mentioning a forest leaders summit and several side events looking at the forest roadmap that have happened during Cop31. “You’re seeing this sort of drumbeat of progress outside the rooms.”
 Despite progress on those fronts, Fernanda de Carvalho, head for Policy and Climate Energy at WWF International said the cover text still matters – and far more needs to be done.
 “We always have hope and we always have to see the positive side of this, but it’s not going well and there is concern,” she said, pointing specifically to the discussions around finance and adaptation that need to be addressed.
 While she was glad that language around the 1.5C overshoot was included, she said it’s been diluted from the first draft. “It would be great if parties could highlight that 1.5 remains the ultimate goal of the convention,” she said. There are also some problematic inclusions, specifically a provision supporting the scaling of global carbon capture, which she called “dangerous”. “We think the numbers are overestimated,” she added, calling it opportunistic and complicated.
 “There’s a Lenny Kravitz principle – it ain’t over till it’s over,” she said. “I’m calling on the double presidency or the presidencies to keep moving and keep striving for consensus.”
 Share Updated at  10.21 EST 23h ago 09.56 EST US, China and Russia agree to pump more oil
 Oliver Milman Several thousand miles away from the negotiating rooms in Antalya, three of the world’s heavyweight powers (and major carbon polluters) have held a rare meeting, with rather ominous outcomes for the climate.
 US president Donald Trump, Chinese president Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin met in trilateral talks held in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. It was all very friendly – Trump greeted Putin by calling him “my friend”, while Xi claimed that the meeting would be focused on “promoting world peace” (the wars waged in Iran and Ukraine by the US and Russia, respectively, were not mentioned in the statement).
 Beyond talks on reforming the UN and curbing the specter of nuclear war, the leaders also committed in a joint statement to boost their output of oil. The US and Russia are among the world’s top oil and gas exporters, while China is the planet’s largest emitter of greenhouse gases. None of the three leaders made the trip to Cop.
 View image in fullscreen Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the Apec summit. Photograph: Win McNamee/Pool Getty Images AsiaPac/AP “The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations,” the statement reads. “They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows.”
 Share Updated at  09.59 EST 23h ago 09.47 EST Joe Pinner ‘I have watched girls in my community lose their dreams because rain did not come’ 
 Every day at Cop31 I’ve been speaking to young climate activists. Today I spoke to Flawa Malle , 25, a climate and gender justice advocate from Tanzania.
 She founded the Eco Pulse Network, which promotes sustainability in schools across the Dodoma region and works with rural women and communities on climate adaptation and locally led solutions.
 View image in fullscreen Flawa Malle (L) founded the Eco Pulse Network in Tanzania. Photograph: Eco Pulse Network “In Tanzania, climate change is not a headline – it is our daily life. When drought comes, farming stops. When farming stops, girls drop out of school because there is no income at home. I have watched girls in my community lose their dreams, not because they lacked talent, but because the rain did not come.
 “That is why I am at Cop31 . I am here to make sure leaders hear what adaptation really looks like.
 “We created the Safaad Girls Tailoring Project because our community needed a solution that works when agriculture is not possible. We used discarded fabrics to teach girls tailoring and income-generating skills. That is adaptation.
 “We started one year ago with three sewing machines and 20 girls. Today we have six machines and 97 girls. But we did this with very little funding. My biggest concern is adaptation finance, especially for youth solutions. Youth are trusted to speak on panels, but not trusted with money.
 “If I could change one thing about Cop, I would make climate finance reach young people directly, without so many barriers. My hope is that Cop31 will not just talk about youth, but fund youth. Because when you fund a girl, you fund a whole community.”
 Share 23h ago 09.36 EST Matthew Pearce Wopke Hoekstra, the European commissioner for climate, net zero and clean growth, and Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, did not comment on how fossil fuels were removed from the draft, telling a huddle of reporters that they would judge the text by whether they can be satisfied that “multilateralism remains capable of delivering progress” and “implementation remained at the centre of international climate action”.
 “We will not be commenting on it now,” they said, telling the press their teams were currently working through it. “We can say that we will judge the content in the context of the mandate we had coming to Antalya as set out in our Council Conclusions.”
 Share 23h ago 09.29 EST Gabrielle Canon View image in fullscreen Activists take part in a demonstration organised by the ActionAid International Foundation during Cop31. Photograph: Kaan Soyturk/Reuters The electrification package was presented on the same day the International Energy Agency (IEA) released its global outlook outlining the “extraordinary uncertainty” caused by the war in Iran and strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions.
 “I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol in a statement issued with the report, adding that the outlook explores what could be in store in the wake of these challenges. “Energy security and energy transitions have never been so closely aligned,” Birol said.
 Energy demand, meanwhile, is only expected to grow fueled by population increases, the rise of AI and the need for cooling as the world warms.
 With these questions – and opportunities – in mind, the push for a transition away from fossil fuels has become deeply linked to the electrification debate, with many parties calling a commitment to renewables within electrification plans and pledges.
 “Governments at Cop31 should explain how their electricity goal will drive down fossil fuel use and bring affordable power to people who still lack it,” Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate and energy thinktank said, pushing for the 35% electrification goal to be tied to renewables. “Governments cannot put a green ribbon around fossil-fired electricity and call it a climate breakthrough.”
 Share 24h ago 09.17 EST Negative reactions to the draft text have been coming in thick and fast. This is from Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at 350.org.
 “We are on the brink of an outrageous and utterly embarrassing lack of leadership by the Cop31 presidencies,” said Sieber. “They have reduced one of the defining challenges of our time to an inconvenient paragraph they would rather delete, while leaving the door open for fossil fuels to masquerade as clean electrification. Last year, Brazil, a country deeply dependent on oil, had the political courage to start confronting the difficult question of how to move beyond fossil fuels. This year with Minister Bowen we got a spineless fossil fuel bro while the Turkey presidency stands by.”
 “Rich countries’ failure on finance is a historic disgrace,” he added. “They expect developing countries to shoulder the costs of a global transition while refusing to provide the means to deliver it. This is not a failure of technical negotiations. It is a shameless abdication of political responsibility. If this is where Cop31 lands, history will remember it as a summit where those entrusted with leadership chose the comfort of inaction over the courage to confront reality.”
 View image in fullscreen Activists from 350.org stage the ‘We are not drowning, we are fighting’ protest during the UN climate summit. Photograph: Antonio Bat/EPA Share Updated at  09.26 EST 24h ago 09.08 EST Panama to block any outcome without a cap on oil production
 Bibi van der Zee Panama has come in with an unusual move; they have sent a letter to the Cop presidency announcing that unless all their demands are met, they will block any outcome. Given that the final agreement must be unanimously agreed, this has powerful implications.
 “We have listened carefully to the speeches of these days,” the delegation writes. “They are beautiful speeches. But while we listen to endless oratory, the planet is being destroyed … Outside this room and this Conference, the world needs and expects radical change from us, and we are not delivering it.”
 View image in fullscreen Panama's environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro signed the letter to the Cop presidency. Photograph: Özge Elif Kızıl/Anadolu/Getty Images “Accordingly, I inform you that Panama will not join any consensus, and will formally object in the closing plenaries, to the adoption of any decision that does not lead to an outcome satisfactory to our principles and our values.” They want to see science as the foundation, real transparency, new rules of engagement, and a cap on oil production, among other things. That last demand will be completely unacceptable to fossil fuel producing countries; even the mention of fossil fuels in the text is problematic for some of them, let alone any suggestion that production should be capped.
 “Panama will not lend its name to an outcome that continues to ignore and attempts to excuse each nation’s individual responsibility, and by so doing prolongs and worsens the crisis,” says the letter. It is signed by Panama’s environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro.
 In the press conference by the Cop presidency, Chris Bowen said – in answer to a question about the letter – that he had not seen it. “We will work the issue through till we have consensus.” That seems optimistic at best.
 Share Updated at  10.01 EST 24h ago 08.59 EST The press conference has come to a slightly abrupt close with the announcement that Cop31 has so far registered just shy of 120,000 participants, 69,000 of whom were on-site.
 Share 1d ago 08.48 EST Questioned on the lack of fossil fuels in the cover decision, Australia’s Chris Bowen has said this Cop is focused on implementation, arguing there is “no better way” than confirming the transition to low greenhouse gas emissions, reaffirming the commitment to keep 1.5C alive, and electrifying the economy.
 “We’ve put forward very concrete proposals in the cover decision, we’re happy to receive feedback.”
 His argument was echoed by Kurum, his Turkish counterpart, who said “we are not here to discuss previous decisions taken”, such as the transition away from fossil fuels agreed at Cop28. The electrification target for 2035, he added, “implies transitioning away from fossil fuels.”
 Kurum rejected the suggestion that there had been any “backsliding” since the first draft, which did mention fossil fuels. Bowen said the purpose of the original wide-ranging draft was “transparency”, so all parties’ views were on the table.
 View image in fullscreen Turkey’s Murat Kurum, left, speaks during a news conference next to Australia’s Chris Bowen. Photograph: Khalil Hamra/AP Share Updated at  08.53 EST 1d ago 08.37 EST “Yes, there are many obstacles, but the Paris agreement is working,” said Simon Stiell, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. He conceded the world is “nowhere near the 1.5C threshold we need to hit” but that the direction had been set, and the hottest futures once expected are no longer on the table. “The issue is speed, or the lack of speed.”
 View image in fullscreen Simon Stiell, United Nations climate chief. Photograph: Khalil Hamra/AP Share Updated at  08.57 EST 1  of  3 Next Oldest Oldest Explore more on these topics Cop31
